# Dear Malik Basintale, What About Those Who Cannot Get Your Attention?

[Silas Bambil · May 2025]{.meta}

Dear Malik Basintale,

I have followed some of your engagements on social media since you became Chief Executive Officer of the Youth Employment Agency, and I find myself increasingly frustrated by what appears to be your approach to public engagement. A prominent personality attracts your attention, a public exchange follows, and an invitation to the offices of the YEA is extended. I appreciate the importance of a public official being responsive to citizens, but these interactions leave me wondering about the young Ghanaians whose concerns will never attract comparable attention. Must their problems become sufficiently popular on social media before they warrant serious consideration?

Can you handle it if we all start tagging you with our problems?

You cannot personally attend to every unemployed graduate or aspiring entrepreneur, nor should you have to. Imagine a young Ghanaian with a promising business proposal but without influential connections, celebrity status, or a substantial social media following. Where does that person go? Who assesses their proposal, and what response can they reasonably expect? Surely, the quality of an idea should matter more than the popularity of the person presenting it. There is a difference between having an accessible Chief Executive Officer and having an accessible institution. I am considerably more interested in the latter.

On 27 May 2025, you publicly expressed interest in partnering with Shatta Wale's ride-hailing business, SHAXI. Three days later, you met him at the offices of the Youth Employment Agency, where you discussed several employment initiatives. Among them was a proposed arrangement involving 150 electric vehicles expected to be brought into the country. During the meeting, you announced that you had instructed your team to have those vehicles registered on SHAXI before assigning drivers to them. Interesting. But there was something about that announcement I genuinely struggled to understand.

What was the original plan for those electric vehicles before you suddenly instructed they be registered under SHAXI?

Had SHAXI already been identified as a suitable platform under an existing employment strategy, or was its selection informed by your recent engagement with Shatta Wale? What criteria informed that decision, and were other arrangements considered? I have absolutely no objection to the Agency partnering with Shatta Wale. His popularity and business activities could contribute positively to employment creation, and I would be delighted to see a Ghanaian-owned ride-hailing business succeed. My concern is whether another entrepreneur with a similarly promising business but considerably less public influence could receive comparable institutional consideration.

The Agency also announced its intention to provide the first 2,000 vehicles joining SHAXI with GH₵500 worth of fuel coupons every month for six months. If all 2,000 vehicles receive the full six months of support, that amounts to a potential subsidy of GH₵6 million, excluding any additional incentives. That is the value implied by the announced terms, not an assertion about money already spent. How will beneficiaries be selected? How many genuinely new employment opportunities will result from this expenditure? What will the beneficiaries earn, and how sustainable will those opportunities be once the subsidies expire?

Perhaps my background in mathematics, finance, and risk management explains my interest in these questions. Registering a vehicle on a ride-hailing platform is not necessarily equivalent to creating a sustainable job. Similarly, identifying the possibility of employing two drivers per vehicle does not establish that both will earn a reasonable living. I want to know what the Agency expects these initiatives to accomplish and how it intends to determine whether those expectations have been realised. An announcement may communicate ambition, but it takes considerably more than an announcement to establish performance.

Then there was your statement of 25 April 2025 concerning the Zoomlion sanitation contract, in which you invoked your late father's grave while pledging not to renew the contract in its existing form. I appreciate your concerns about sanitation workers receiving GH₵250 monthly under that arrangement. But why did an administrative decision concerning the terms of a public contract require such a dramatic personal declaration? Surely, the evidence, contractual obligations, and welfare of the affected workers should provide sufficient grounds for your decision. With all due respect to the memory of your late father, I would rather have confidence in the institutional processes governing your decisions than in the solemnity with which you announce them.

Malik, the president didn’t appoint you CEO to play social media influencer. You’re not running a reality show, and this isn’t group therapy. I understand that public communication is an important aspect of leadership, but the visibility of your activities should not become confused with their effectiveness. Photographs with celebrities, enthusiastic announcements, and favourable reactions on social media tell me remarkably little about whether unemployed young Ghanaians are becoming financially independent. I would be far more interested in knowing how many people have obtained sustainable employment through the Agency's programmes, what those programmes have cost, and whether they have achieved their intended objectives.

I sometimes wonder what impression these highly publicised engagements might leave on ordinary Ghanaians. Suppose a young entrepreneur begins to believe that attracting your attention on social media is more effective than submitting a proposal through the appropriate institutional channels. What would you expect that person to do? Spend more time developing the quality of their proposal or developing the popularity of their social media account? It would be rather unfortunate if, alongside our academic qualifications, professional credentials, and business skills, young Ghanaians also felt compelled to acquire a substantial following on X to improve our prospects of receiving assistance from a public institution.

This matters to me personally. I know the frustration of investing years in education and professional development while struggling to obtain opportunities through which to demonstrate one's abilities. I know what it means to have qualifications, ambitions, and a genuine willingness to work without knowing where the next opportunity will come from. I do not expect the government to provide every young Ghanaian with a job. However, I expect the opportunities offered by public institutions to be reasonably accessible and governed by transparent procedures. Surely, wanting an opportunity should not also require knowing how to get the attention of the person responsible for providing it.

I recognise that the Youth Employment Agency already has mechanisms for facilitating employment, including its Job Centre. My concern is how effectively these arrangements serve ordinary Ghanaians. At some point, somebody else will occupy your office. Will young people then have to familiarise themselves with another personality, discover what attracts that person's attention, and devise new ways of getting their concerns heard? I want you to strengthen an institution whose procedures are sufficiently clear and reliable that a young Ghanaian can obtain assistance without even needing to know the name of its Chief Executive Officer.

Malik, I genuinely want you to succeed. Your success could mean that thousands of young Ghanaians become capable of supporting themselves, helping their parents, establishing families, and pursuing ambitions they have spent years postponing. By all means, engage with Shatta Wale and other prominent individuals whose businesses can contribute to employment creation. But remember that some of the most promising ideas may come from people whose names you have never heard, whose social media posts will never trend, and whose arrival at the offices of the Youth Employment Agency will never attract a single camera.

They are young Ghanaians, too.

You have demonstrated that you can make yourself accessible to people who can get your attention. What I would really love to see is an institution that works equally well for those who cannot.

With respect,

SB

*This open letter was inspired by the public engagements and employment initiatives announced by Ghana's Youth Employment Agency in 2025.*
